#4019. EA execs choosing Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 was the main factor in BioWare's demise, according to report

Corporate chair shuffling and the Mass Effect studio's recent struggles may also have played roles

The postmortem on BioWare, following their shuttering by EA this month, points to the publisher's preference to back Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 as the main factor in the demise of the beloved RPG developer. That's according to Bloomberg, who also report that a couple of other factors likely also had some influence.

The Bloomberg report paints EA's position as being one of a company caught between spending a bunch of money on a Star Wars shooter-shaped rock and a hard place with a sign that read Mass Effect 5. Disney reportedly swooped in to offer the publishers the opportunity to make Star Wars Battlefront 3 around the time EA were, as a result of being saddled with debt as part of the leveraged buyout which saw the Saudi government and private equity take them over, looking to not to spend as much cash.

So, Star Wars and Mass Effect became a decision of whether Star Wars or Mass Effect would be the better bet to stick projected hundreds of millions of dollars on. The suits, quelle surprise really, went for the series that currently sits just below powerhouse money-maker Winnie the Pooh on Wikipedia's list of the highest-grossing media franchises. Battlefront 3's development reportedly hasn't even kicked off yet, but it's got that safe and predictable big name to it, and will be a shooter to nestle among EA's treasured flotilla of gun and ball games, rather than an RPG.

Bloomberg add that that BioWare's well-documented up and down record with game releases since Mass Effect: Andromeda began a skid which Anthem only made worse and Dragon Age: The Veilguard couldn't arrest also played a role. Potentially also in the mix was some corporate chair and nameplate switching among EA's execs this summer, which saw EA Sports-linked suits David Tinson and Cam Weber promoted while reported BioWare advocate Laura Miele was sidelined via promotion from overseeing EA's non-sports studios to a gig based around helping big boss Andrew Wilson pursue "strategic growth opportunities beyond EA's core business".

For what it's worth, an EA spokesperson told Bloomberg the company "collectively" decided to shoot BioWare into space "following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities".

And so, BioWare's body has been sent to the stars, while Respawn and DICE look set to make Battlefront 3. There is a bit of depressing irony in EA deciding to go for the perceived safe bet of a big name licensed game over taking some risk on a game that'd come without Disney as a rights-holding middleman. This is, after all, the company which in 2022 ditched governing body Fifa as the namesake and licensing partner of their very successful football games, choosing the risk of going it alone with a lesser brand EA would have more direct control over and ownership of rather than sticking with an established big name juggernaut.

Then again, you could probably call EA's soccer games something like 'Hey, you, person reading this: the (insert year here) football game you're looking at thinks your face is ugly and your haircut's stupid' and they'd still fly off the shelves.

Ultima creator Richard Garriott was one of several developers on a recent panel hosted by the Georgia Game Developers Association, and Lord British was in fine form. Calling himself the "great-grandpa" of the group, he began by summarizing the current problems faced by the videogame industry.

"It's not just one thing," Garriott began. "I think if it was one thing it would be a lot easier to diagnose and come back from, but it's a lot of folks who don't understand videogames trying to make money off of videogames, it's a political climate, it's a billion things. All the threads have woven together into this horrible knot that we're seeing now."

He went on to describe a cycle he's seen play out multiple times over his years in the industry, where a technological advance comes along and everyone races to make a simple game that highlights that advance—whether it's the CD-ROM or a 3D-rendering pipeline or the internet—and only in the short gaps between these leaps forward is there much demand for something deeper.

"That cycle has been normal," Garriott said. "But we're at a new one, and this new one is machines are now fast enough to where the bells and whistles are no longer what's important." Without another advance having the same impact, he said, "we're at this kind of creative cliff where I think people don't know exactly what to do to prevent it and I think we've lost a lot of the original creators that were associated with those IPs and the bigger companies, and so I think we're floundering."

Garriott also had something to say about the way publishers have responded to the current state of the industry—by canceling games and laying off staff. Referring to his own publisher, Origin Systems, which he sold to EA in 1992, Garriott said, "Origin pre-EA, we never cancelled a project. Our theory was that if that team is capable of getting across the finish line, even if it doesn't sell well, they'll now know what it feels like to finish. And they will get feedback from the sales and the public as to what they did and didn't do right and so that team will be more strong, the individuals will be stronger, and we'll be able to circle back and do a more competent game next time.

"If you cancel a project, that means all those people on that team think you the publisher suck, because obviously their idea must've been brilliant, and so your willingness to cancel it was not their fault, but you the evil publisher. And half of them are probably going to leave or get fired, and maybe you'll scoop a few of them over into some other project that's now the priority project, but we thought that was a bad move on our own."

Things changed once EA snapped up Origin and took control, however. After that? "We canceled more projects than we completed by a long shot," Garriott said.

#4016. Capcom's golden streak continues as Onimusha and Pragmata sell well, but Monster Hunter Wilds conspicuously absent from financial report

Capcom has revealed updated sales figures for its new and successful games, including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Pragmata, and Resident Evil Requiem. But for some reason, Monster Hunter Wilds is absent from the report.

Capcom's half-year report, for the period running 1st April to 30th September, saw growth in both revenue and profit across nearly all segments of the business. In games, much of that was driven by digital sales, which continue to account for the vast majority of the publisher's income.

The first half of FY2026 was especially strong for Capcom owing to the release of multiple critically acclaimed and financially successful titles. Onimusha: Way of the Sword has now sold over 1.7m copies, up from the 1m it sold at launch. Pragmata, another critical and financial hit, has grown its tally to 2.7m copies, more than double what it sold in its first two days of release. Resident Evil Requiem, meanwhile, has now surpassed 8.5m copies sold.

As part of the same report, Capcom also recorded its highest-ever number of unit sales for the first half of any fiscal year. This is attributed to Capcom's strong back-catalogue of titles, and regular sales and discounts.

But Capcom did not reference Monster Hunter Wilds sales at all in the report. The publisher did not share updated sales for the game, despite sharing a milestone for predecessor Monster Hunter: World, which is now well past 30m copies sold.

Although Wilds was incredibly successful at launch, the game's player base tapered off dramatically shortly afterwards. Capcom offered a sales update in last year's version of the same report, where it was revealed that MH Wilds had sold close to 11m copies overall, but the publisher hasn't offered an update since.

What does this mean - have sales slowed so significantly as to not be worth mentioning? Perhaps. But given that Wilds is coming to Switch 2 this December, and with the Ascendance expansion due for release next year, there's fuel in the tank yet.

#4015. Wooshy wuxia actioner Phantom Blade Zero is sharp enough on the Steam Machine, if blunted on the Steam Deck

It would appear that Phantom Blade Zero (Phantom Blade 0? Zero? Let’s go with Zero) demanding more gigs than a mismanaged stadium is doing little to stop people playing the thing. It therefore stands to reason at least some folks will want to run S-Game Studio’s lightly Soulsy sword-em-up on the Steam Machine, so let us now examine how said GabeCube stands up to its effects-heavy martial artistry. With some settings proposals, natch.

Two signs boded poorly, before I got to testing the Machine. The first was a comment on Oisin’s day one patch piece, warning of heavy glitching on a Linux system. The second was my Steam Deck OLED, also a Linux system, being incapable of running Phantom Blade Zero at even close to a steady 30fps; even with the Low preset and some nasty-looking Ultra Performance upscaling, the game’s flashy moves and jerking (apologies – cinematic) camera shifts made for regular framerate drops into the teens.

Fortunately, the Steam Machine is much more resilient, even if it does benefit from a few quality cuts (and, realistically, will struggle if pushed beyond standard 1080p.) The Medium preset and Quality-level FSR are enough for 45-60fps in what I’ve played so far, and the High preset – while a touch susceptible to sub-40fps dips for my liking – is at least playable without major bugs or stuttering.

Strangely enough, the only major technical problem I’ve had wasn’t caused by graphics, or the Linux-based SteamOS, but the Steam Controller I was playing with. Despite being assured during the boot process that I was being treated to the Official Gamepad Configuration – cor! – an unresponsive map-opening button left me immobile during a prompt tutorial. Immobile and, I suppose without a map, lost. It turns out this this is a common bug with the Steam Controller specifically, and can be fixed by remapping the Select button, in SteamOS’s controller settings, to emulate the effect of clicking the touchpad of a PS5 pad. PC gaming.

With that sorted, Phantom Blade Zero seems to work fine? If I was nitpicking I’d point out that some high-drama sequences are visibly less buttery than the slower, roaming sections, which can exceed 60fps on Medium. Same for a lot of cutscenes, which aren’t hard-locked to 30fps like prerendered scenes often are, but do cause heavy framerate drops for little apparent reason. Still, it’s reasonable when actually playing.

Settings-wise, that Medium preset (with FSR on Quality) works well if you’re lazy. But a few of Phantom Blade Zero’s individual quality options aren’t terribly performance-sapping by themselves, and than thus be tuned upwards for a slightly nicer-looking wuxia tale with minimal drawback. Have a crack with the following:

Don’t miss those Dynamic Resolution Quality and Super Resolution Output Scale tweaks; on their defaults, they both make the game uglier than it needs to be. And on the subject of Super Resolution, FSR upscaling does leave a bit of roughness on certain edges, but then at 1080p, so does FSR even when it’s on its Native Resolution setting. You might as well get the extra frames.

For a period of the PS5 generation, Sony ported its games to the PC, rendering very few of its titles genuine exclusives.

In the last year and a bit it’s made an internal decision to focus solely on exclusivity, and it’s slowly beginning to promote that again.

As spotted by power user Radec on social media, the official PlayStation.com pages for Ghost of Yotei and Until Dawn 2 now include ‘PlayStation Exclusive’ logos.

While the manufacturer experimented with bringing its first-party titles to Steam, sales were allegedly poor.

This proves the company is now doubling down on exclusivity again, although it has said it’ll continue to release select multiplayer and live service games on PC, such as this year’s Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls.

I imagine we’re going to see Sony start to tout the ‘PlayStation Exclusive’ branding more aggressively once it rebuilds its library, beginning with next year’s God of War Laufey and (hopefully) Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet.

#4013. Here are our PS Plus monthly games for November 2026

Dead Island 2! Tomb Raider! Monster Train 2!

Sony has announced the monthly games coming to PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra next month, bringing a mix of triple-A bangers and remastered classics to the service on the 3rd November. All are, of course, coming at the start of what is almost certainly going to be the biggest month of the year releases-wise.

Perhaps the biggest game on offer is Dead Island 2, Dambuster Studios and Deep Silver's first person zombie action game. There's plenty of grisly goodness here, and ample loot to snatch up and use against the undead hordes. It's a decent enough game, which should offer plenty of entertainment to those looking for something chunky to dig their teeth into while the Halloween spirit still lingers.

The remastered Tomb Raider Darkness Trilogy is not one to be skipped, especially if you're looking for a sizable time sink from your PlayStation Plus monthly games. While not known as being exactly the best Lara Croft games out there, Aspyr did some fine work polishing them up for modern platforms.

Finally we've got Monster Train 2. A deckbuilder roguelike that has you operating and managing trains where the forces of heaven and hell reside, all to defeat titans that threaten the orderly state of things. As the sole indie release on this monthly selection of PlayStation Plus games, it may be worth a try for those who can't get enough from the Roguelike genre even now. It even features a smug looking mushroom fella, how can you go wrong with that.

The reveal of these games coming to PlayStation Plus means the clock is ticking to grab October's offerings, many of which would fit well on the console of those getting into the spooky season.

For more information on PlayStation Plus, you can check out our guide to PS Plus and all the available games here.

Which of these three games have caught your eye?

#4012. Warframe's fantasy-pilled sister Soulframe finally goes open to all this November, though Digital Extremes are "nervous" about certain changes

They're celebrating the end of closed alpha by poisoning the world

Warframe creators Digital Extremes have announced that their free-to-play fantasy RPG Soulframe will be available for everyone to download on 6th November, after two years in closed alpha. Finally, you serfs without "prelude" keys will be able to fire up Soulframe.com and make sense of my ranting about the sleeping animals on the lobby screen.

The new "open prelude" will land shortly before the game's 17th major update, Verse of the Veilands, which lets you grow your Omen wolfpup allies into rideable adult wolves by finding the ingredients for a special biscuit. More importantly, prelude 17 violently rearranges the game's wistful world, adding an Ubisoft-esque region purging system that is designed to guide new players a bit more emphatically towards the game's "votives". Aka, missions. Yes, Digital Extremes sort of have a bespoke term for every game feature in Soulframe. I find this can be either charming or maddening, depending on how much sleep I've had.

Here's how the region purging will work: after completing the game's Tormented Stag quest, you'll find that the landscape is being corrupted by siphons deployed by the villainous star-faring Ode faction. You have to complete votives to build energy and learn the sacred song of each region, allowing you to cleanse it and restore the environment.

In a roundtable preview session last week, creative director Geoff Crookes and lead designer Scott McGregor expressed a certain amount of anxiety about deliberately polluting Soulframe's fairytale ambience. "Scott and I were just talking yesterday about, aesthetically, how nervous we are about this change," Crookes commented, "because the game has gotten a lot of really great feedback on how cosy it is, how beautiful the world is, and you're going to enter a game that is much more unforgiving and harsh at first glance."

That said, he thinks the shift "pairs really well with going into open alpha, because it is a much stronger breadcrumb [trail] for the player, to pull them into the world and give them a bit more ownership of what they're doing." Once rinsed of Ode siphons, regions will appear more like how they are in previous versions of Soulframe, with activities such as fishing and new resources to snaffle.

McGregor added that hitherto, a lot of Soulframe players have gotten lost and put the game down after completing the opening "Fables", or story quests. "It's a really big change to the structural flow of the game, you know," he told the assembled journorabble. "We're very open and discoverable, and we had a lot of player feedback that was basically 'what do I do next? What do I do next? I don't know what to do next'.

"So [it's] taking that and mashing it with the votive system, which is our mission system for the game, and making that more of a directed experience," he went on, "and then once they get through that directed experience, they can go back to that open world." Prelude 17 will also let you accept votives more straightforwardly from the world map, after finding the local representative or mission giver.

Digital Extremes have a new Soulframe "pact" or character loadout on the boil, the Ode Shrike. It's a dastardly poacher class who specialises in spike traps and throwable bolas. The Shrike's standout ability is a balloon dart that lets you hoist enemies into the sky, as in Metal Gear Solid V.

You can read more about Soulframe's on-going reinventions on the official site. While you won't need a key to get access as of Nov 6th, the game's paid Founders program will remain the same. Digital Extremes will likely still run closed preview builds alongside the "open prelude", testing out features with a smaller group of players. They're also looking into giving you the ability to reset your character, so you can check out any new material added to parts of the game you've finished.

I'm not sure I've ever been exhilarated by Soulframe, but I like the poise, flamboyance and gentle complexity of its combat. I also really enjoy its faded tapestry aesthetics, though I think it's yanking on the goo-goo glands too avidly with all these fluffy forest animals. Enough photogenic wolfpups, Digital Extremes - let's see you make, I don't know, a blobfish look adorable.

It's also very interesting as a new live service project from a company defined by the success of Warframe. I spoke to the Soulframe developers earlier in the year about the challenge of borrowing Warframe's thunder without getting lost in its shadow.

#4011. "This company has been driven into a wall for years" - Life is Strange studio Don't Nod faces unrest while teetering on insolvency

"For two years, employees have been living on the edge."

There's deep unrest at French studio Don't Nod - creator of Life is Strange, Remember Me, Vampyr, Banishers: New Eden, and most recently Aphelion - as it scrambles to restructure itself and guard against insolvency.

Indeed, an impassioned account of proceedings on French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo's website (via Rock, Paper, Shotgun) reveals Don't Nod has entered safeguard proceedings - a kind of last-ditch restructuring effort to stave off insolvency. It also reports that even though redundancies are being made,Don't Nod intends to finish making the in-development game codenamed P14, albeit relying more on outsourced development rather than its cut-down in-house team.

The report, which claims knowledge of a memo sent by Don't Nod CEO Oskar Guilbert, and of the goings-on of the Don't Nod employee representatives - the CSE - doubts whether Don't Nod will be able to finish the game. Apparently all of the studio's character artists, concept artists, most of its environment artists, most of its sound designers, game designers, level designers, programmers, producers, testers, and dev-ops have been let go.

"To compensate for this massacre and keep on running with production on a game that, to this day, didn't cut down on its scope and is keeping around a hundred persons busy, management is betting it all on outsourcing," the report says.

"Managers, who are usually seen as more competent and experienced than non-managers, are kept within the organisation and studio management expects them to orchestrate the massive shift to outsourcing as well as take over the workload of the fired team members. Anyone with a little experience with video games production and sanity understands how out-of-touch such a plan is."

The report also claims Don't Nod management isn't able to offer affected staff severance packages or redundancy plans. "It'll be the strict legal minimum and you'll be glad for it," the report said. A voluntary redundancy scheme also isn't reportedly being offered.

"This company has been driven into a wall for years, against all outsider wisdom, against any sort of reality-based assessment," the report went on. "For two years, employees have been living on the edge, in uncertainty and anxiety, all of it reinforced by internal comms that alternated between inexistence and outright lies. This impacted their health, as evidenced by the CSE who documented six workplace accidents in 2026 and recently had to launch an inquiry into a serious and imminent danger.

"They do not care about the damage it deals to employees' health, they made no risk prevention plan. Employees feel like hostages to a radicalised management, who keep playing with the livelihood and the future of 140 people with no care for the consequences of their actions."

The CSE negotiations apparently end on 3rd November. We've asked Don't Nod for a comment.

News of Don't Nod's slide towards the brink of insolvency comes a month after the company's board voted to enter a period of restructuring - of transformation - that could lead to lay-offs for as many as 90 people. That in turn came only a few months after Don't Nod said it was close to running out of money.

The company's most recent game, Aphelion (released in April) - which charted a duo's escape across a sci-fi world - struggled to find an audience. We didn't review it on Eurogamer but a brief look around shows it only received middling scores. 2025's Life is Strange follow-up Lost Records fared better - we awarded it four out of five stars - but its success wasn't enough to properly propel the studio.

#4010. What are we all playing this weekend?

My scares should have been reserved for today, what with it being All Hallows' Eve and all, but my fright came on Thursday.

It was a dark October night and I was returning from work. A storm had blown through earlier in the week, so the evening was unusually crisp and clear. I walked between the terrace houses, feeling the eyes of work-from-homers on my back. I turned the key in the door to the communal hallway, climbed the creaky stairs, and tried to keep my footsteps light as I passed my rude neighbour's flat. My head was wholly absorbed by the prospect of the risotto I had waiting in the fridge/

I unlocked my front door and started up the internal staircase to the kitchen, not even bothering to turn on the lights. Out of the dark, something jumped down the stairs at me, hitting me in the stomach. I flicked the lights on in a panic and saw a small brown thing with a long tail bolting back up the staircase. A mouse. In my house.

Terrifying stuff, I'm sure you will agree. It almost put me off my risotto. Anyway, this is what the rest of the team will be up to this weekend..

OllieI've settled into a very comfy rhythm of playing the latest Trackmania campaign and also a bit of Factorio, both with my brother. When I've a bit of time to myself I'm also interested in trying out Queen's Domain. Heard good things!

JeremyI continue to chip away at our Castlevania walkthrough as it chips away at my soul. Such is the transactional bargain of dealing with Dracula during Halloween, no? However, as I answer the door for trick-or-treaters, I may partake in what is becoming an annual tradition - watching an old game playthrough on YouTube as I hand out sweets. I'm thinking I will watch the 1994 SNES game Nosferatu this year, which is not related to Castlevania but does feature a bold guy going to beat up Dracula and all of his minions with nothing but his feet and fists.

JamesMy previously mentioned attempts to play Mortal Shell 2 have been thwarted this week by, in chronological order, work, social obligations, brownie making, Deep Rock Galactic, and more brownie making. We go again.

EdwinI'm helping with a house move this weekend, so I doubt I'll have much time for your foolish computer entertainments, but I'd like to crack on with Queen's Domain and also, try out Danchi Days, a sorrowful comedy about trying to revive a summer festival in a 2000s-era Japanese neighbourhood.

CallumSuspiciously, Callum has been making squeaking noises in meetings. Is this a sign he planted the mouse? Perhaps he was the mouse. Surely, it's not a coincidence. There's no such thing as coincidence when it comes to mice.

MarkI want to finish Virtue and a Sledgehammer, having started it the other night. I really dug The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood, one of Spanish studio Deconstructeam's previous games. Thus far, VaaS is hitting just as hard in terms of emotional beats, but in a manner that's more haunting than charming. We'll see where I land on it by the end.

JulianAs well as searching my flat for mouse hidey holes, I will be (touch wood/cross fingers/make a sacrifice to Bob the Builder) finishing the DIY I started last weekend. Alcove bookcases and a painted living room are in my future, I just have to manifest it.

Besides that, I've been dipping my toes into Titanium Court. I like it but I don't so far love it. It's witty, the presentation is excellent, but I feel like it is also keeping me at arm's length and I want to be drawn into its world, not kept at a distance. It may just need more time. I will also be trying hard not to sweep the moon.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earlier this year, Electronic Arts was snapped up by a consortium including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and the investment firms Silver Lake and Affinity Partners in a deal worth $55 billion. According to Reuters, now the PIF and Silver Lake have their sights set on Unity Software, the company behind the multiplatform game engine of the same name.

Silver Lake is already one of Unity's bigger shareholders, owning roughly 8% of the company since investing around $400 million in it back in 2017. "Silver ​Lake’s Egon Durban also sits ⁠on Unity's board," as Reuters notes, "a dual role that would typically lead him to recuse himself from board deliberations on a sale."

The deliberations so far apparently include a valuation of about $25 billion, though since then Unity's most recent earnings report has come in, showing profits higher than estimated. Unity's come a long way since the Runtime Fee scandal, but it's not all about improvements to the engine like its ability to integrate with Unreal. As Reuters reports, "Strong ⁠growth in Unity's AI-powered Vector advertising platform helped it post its first quarterly profit on a GAAP basis since going public in September 2020."

The first thing that happened to EA after it was acquired was mass layoffs and being saddled with $18 billion of debt. I can't imagine anyone actually working at Unity has their fingers crossed for this deal to go through, but the videogame industry does seem determined to speedrun its way into a consolidation crisis where three consortiums own everything and almost everyone is unemployed.

#4008. Feature: Going Platinum: For About Two Months, I Was a Devout Member of the Cult of the Lamb

Hello. Been a minute since the last one, I know, but about 15,000 games have launched in the last few weeks, and Going Platinum sort of fell by the wayside.

But I'm determined to pick up where I left off, and I left off at Cult of the Lamb, a game I was totally enraptured by for a good couple of months.

It's a curious case for me, this one. One half of the game is right up my street (the roguelike action part) and the other half sort of isn't at all (the crafting, survival, management part).

For that reason I probably shouldn't have liked it nearly as much as I did, but the combination of all its elements together is pretty much perfect.

It does something I love to see in games, where every singular aspect of the design feeds into something else.

Going out on a run allows you to gather resources and recruit new members to your cult, then you return home and improve your settlement, which in turn makes you gradually more powerful.

Both parts of the game are quite simple in their execution, but you're never at a loss for things to do; there are new buildings to construct, a new boss to defeat, new followers to brainwash. It's an extremely compelling cycle that I really loved.

It helps that it has a great art style and cartoonish charm that takes the edge off of its dark humour. It's extremely well executed across the board, really — I'm not surprised it's Devolver Digital's biggest game ever.

As for the Trophy hunt, it's another pretty straightforward one. The platinum is surprisingly rare; at the time of writing, only 1.8 per cent of players have unlocked it on the PS5 version.

Looking through the list, it seems the biggest hurdles for people are just collecting things. There are Trophies for getting all the tarot cards, follower skins, and fleeces, and fewer people have unlocked those than have beaten all the bosses without taking damage.

In any case, it's a very fun game, and an enjoyable plat. It took me just under two months, and I really loved every moment.

Do you have the platinum Trophy for Cult of the Lamb? Tell us in the comments section below.

Stephen has been part of the Push Square team for over six years, bringing boundless enthusiasm and a deep knowledge of video games to his role as Assistant Editor. Having grown up playing every PlayStation console to date, he's developed an eclectic taste, with particular passion for indie games, arcade racers, and puzzlers. He's also our go-to guy for Sonic-related matters, much to his delight/chagrin.

#4007. Cyberpunk 2 might include multiplayer after CD Projekt Red scrapped the feature in Cyberpunk 2077

Cyberpunk 2 might try to revive Cyberpunk 2077's online ambitions, as a new CD Projekt Red job listing is looking for someone familiar with "multiplayer network architecture."

As spotted by Cheap Happens, the role-playing powerhouse is currently looking to hire a lead quest programmer for its upcoming open-world sequel. Buried away at the bottom of the job listing, under the "Nice To Haves" section, the studio asks for an "understanding of multiplayer network architecture and client-server synchronization for game state/ quests."

The multiplayer mention is by no means confirmation that Cyberpunk 2 - or whatever it ends up being called - will have co-op and other online modes, but it's definitely something CD Projekt Red is looking into. And it certainly makes sense, too.

Once upon a time, Cyberpunk 2077 was intended to receive a multiplayer portion sometime after its initial launch. Of course, at the time, the shaky state of the game's development meant that was no longer feasible and CD Projekt Red instead said multiplayer would come as its own "triple-A release." Eventually, the famed studio realised it simply had to focus on ensuring the base game was stable enough on its own, and shelved those online ambitions.

A few years back, Cyberpunk 2077's senior quest designer, Philipp Weber, told Eurogamer the company was "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day" by "building an online technology that can be seamlessly integrated into development of our future games."

More recently, in 2024, CD Projekt CEO Adam Badowski said the team were "considering" multiplayer elements for the Cyberpunk sequel back when the game was still in its early concept phases.

We don't know much else about the neon-drenched follow-up, but CDPR has been keeping series fans full and fed with continual updates to Cyberpunk 2077. Earlier this week, the game got an update celebrating the debut of Cyberpunk Edgerunners Season 2 on Netflix - everything from dual-wielding to cross-platform mods were added to the six-year-old game.

#4006. Horror-steeped card game Forbidden Solitaire shows how a strong theme can elevate even decade-old mechanics

Like a tag team of oiled snakes that have entered a wrestling contest, theme is a difficult quality to pin down. A game can be well designed, but if it lacks a coherence between those mechanics and its appearance, narrative, and its framing, there is a dissonance that can be hard to ignore. I realise I've just stepped into an old argument by using the word 'dissonance', but Hocking was right, games that don't cohere can be jarring. A developer may desire that sensation of discomfort, but often it is accidental and unwanted.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

(Much like opening an article with a simile about wrestling snakes when there is nothing connecting that image to a game about solitaire. It might be a good line, but it doesn't smoothly connect with the rest of the article to elevate its argument.)

Anyway, what does this all have to do with Forbidden Solitaire, a game in which you're delving deeper into a dungeon filled with horrors, progressing by clearing screens of cards? Well, it's an excellent example of how well-handled theming can raise a game into something more than its parts.

I've been playing Grey Alien Games' work since they released Regency Solitaire in 2015, and their games often revolve around the same core, Solitaire-inspired mechanics. Each level is a screen filled with stacks of playing cards, and you must clear the screen by picking cards that are one higher or lower than the one currently in your hand. In addition to standard playing cards, you may find padlock cards which can only be cleared with a matching key card, special cards that reshuffle all the stacks, or ones that change cards into suits or numbers that may help you. Except, in each of their games – Regency Solitaire, Shadowhand, Ancient Enemy, and now Forbidden Solitaire - the scenario for those mechanics changes, and in doing do, they show the power of recontextualising.

In Forbidden Solitaire, you're playing a game within a game. Although it's set in 2019, your character is playing a 1995 CD-ROM they found in a second-hand shop. It's one you vaguely remember from your childhood, if mainly for the controversy it caused at launch. The game sees you breaking into an old dungeon and exploring its depths. Each locked door that blocks you, labyrinth that puzzles you, or enemy that challenges you is tackled with the mechanics of Grey Alien Games' previous releases: screens of stacked cards to be cleared. Even familiar special cards, such as the one which shuffles all the cards before you, make a return. As you progress through Forbidden Solitaire's dungeon, you're interrupted by messages from your sister in the present, who is researching the game and the controversy surrounding it, sending you links to police reports, old news clips of the secretive developer, and hidden documents on a centuries-old group of cultists.

Yet, despite the mechanical familiarity, it's this fresh theme that elevates Forbidden Solitaire into something special. For new players, the 1995 game framing device immediately gives an allowance for the simple card mechanics, and allows them to sink into the kitsch horror story of cult members developing haunted video games. But, for returning players like me, I can see all the neat ways the old tools have been adapted to fit this new world. When you find a person marked for sacrifice tied to a bed, for instance, the level to free them is filled with locks that only disappear when you match enough cards of the same suit. It's a pairing of unlocking mechanics that have been in Grey Alien Games' work for at least the past decade to a moment in the story where you are untying a character. The action dovetails with the narrative perfectly.

Anyway, when I realised the role that theme had to play in Forbidden Solitaire, I was feeling extremely smart and smug. Then I reread Adam (RPS in peace) and Pip's (RPS in peace) Regency Solitaire verdict from 2015.

Adam: I think the whole game is a superb example of how a decent design can be elevated by a strong theme. It’s not even particularly overindulgent - flourishes throughout but no extended dialogues or huge slabs of exposition. It’s a few attractive backgrounds (though with an inaccurate non-pebbled Brighton beach, I’m told by RPS chatroom stalwart and Brighton denizen Alec Meer), a handful of characters and miniature conversations to set the tone. But it’s all done so well. It seems to be aware of its own posture in a way that allows it to be well-mannered, well-meaning and not at all over-bearing.

If it had been pixies or space marines, I don’t think I’d have been particularly interested at all - and that’s not to say the actual card game isn’t well-constructed because it is - but even though the story is slight, it’s a great reward at the end of a few hands.

Pip: I'd agree with that, particularly about the setting. It's a game that has a good understanding of its own size, scope and the tone which suits it.

Those absolute cads. Still, go play Forbidden Solitaire anyway. It's a far better time than trying to get an oiled snake into a three-piece suit.

#4005. Alien: Isolation 2 devs commit to a physical edition: "Staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our pillars"

And the Xenomorph's "even more intelligent" this time.

The developers behind Alien: Isolation 2 are committing to a full physical edition, and have shared even more details about the highly-anticipated survival horror sequel.

In a recent developer Q&A posted today (below), developers from Creative Assembly shed even more light on their shadowy follow-up to 2014's fan-favorite horror game. When asked if the sequel would get a physical edition, the devs simply said "yes" and explained that "staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our pillars."

Throughout the video, the Creative Assembly team reiterated that so much of their inspiration comes from Ridley Scott's seminal sci-fi classic from 1979, naturally, which influenced their decision to release a physical boxed version of the game and to keep the focus on one ever present, highly intelligent and always frightening Xenomorph.

Confirmation of a physical release comes months after Sony announced plans to end production of new PlayStation discs in 2028 - a decision that led to heated backlash from players, physical distributors and consumer rights groups.

The only wrinkle is that Alien: Isolation 2 doesn't have a release date at the moment. Should it release any later than February, 2028, PlayStation players probably won't be able to get their hands on a proper disc - though the game is also launching across PC, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X/S.

Elsewhere in the dev vlog, creative director Al Hope explained how the team is expanding on the original game's famously tight level design. "You have the interior spaces which feel claustrophobic and the player feels trapped, which is super familiar to Isolation fans. But we also have exteriors as well where the creature is now learning to adapt and hunt in these open spaces," Hope said.

"I really love the idea that the player will feel trapped and claustrophobic in the interiors and actually really want to get outside. Once they manage to do that, after that initial relief and sense of a small victory, they will start very slowly to feel really exposed and vulnerable and actually quite like to go back inside again. And really, playing on that roller coaster and see-saw of emotion and motivation - that's a big part of what Alien: Isolation 2 is."

James Green, lead game designer, also said roughly "a quarter to a third of the team worked on the original," while all new developers helped to bring a fresh perspective onboard. And, somehow, the Xenomorph is "even more intelligent" this time; scarily capable of using the extreme climate to hide and hunt you.

#4004. The Sunday Papers

Sundays are for looking upon my DIY works and despairing. Strewn sawdust, spilled paint, and hunks of broken MDF litter my living room kingdom. When will it be over? When will I be free? When will I be able to reassemble my sofa, sit down with a cup of tea in hand, and admire my books, unpacked and arranged on perfectly fitted alcove bookshelves?

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

"Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

Inside our Gchat walls, there is a growing exhaustion with genAI stories. Every day another gaming boss talks about the inexorable march of the tech before putting out a trailer filled with blurry text and six-fingered characters. I don't doubt the tech is getting better, but it's not inevitable. As such, Rob Fahey's latest GI column is something of a balm:

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.

A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

Doesn't it feel like everything — especially everything Big Tech touches — is getting worse? Generative AI, not merely content with robbing humans of our craft and jobs, has escaped containment into physical reality in the form of shitty event flyers and small business signage. Hugely profitable industries like video games and film are being torn apart by the financialization of the economy as shareholders seek ever-increasing short-term profits. Algorithmic pricing of rent and groceries threatens to further punish the working class for the crime of not being born rich.

But in the heart of despair, we must reach for that which is good and pure and — dare I say it — better than it used to be. Karaoke is one of those things. And it is better not because of the disruption of tech giants, but, as is often the case, thanks to the work of enterprising maniacs toiling in obscurity, purely out of the love of the game.

I've been playing Forbidden Solitaire this week, where FMV sequences starring Xalavier Nelson Jr as an obsessive fantasy-author-turned-video-game-developer are played for laughs. So it was with a minor sense of whiplash I read Ashley Bardhan's piece for This Week In Video Games. Bardhan speaks to horror developers inserting themselves into FMV games to confront and explore violence against women.

Cara Cadaver uses her own photos and videos to represent multiple victims of sexual violence and murder in her unflinching 2025 game Vile: Exhumed. She tells me over email, “Being a woman is inherently a horrifying and violent experience, any way you slice it. One of my inspirations for making games in general is pulling from real-life experience and telling stories that most every woman has lived in some way; that’s real horror.”

“Horror in general has been a major outlet for me while dealing with trauma, and so much of horror as a genre goes back to women,” Cadaver says. “Women’s stories belong in horror — and that has been the case as long as horror has existed.”

Over at RPS-but-it's-The-Fade, Brendan's run through what made Bioware games great (and also terrible).

Bioware established romance as a must for any blockbuster RPG worth its frost salts (and not just RPGs).

Kissing your friends on the mouth is everywhere in mainstream and indie games today. It's a verb now. Characters are "romanceable". I played Nivalis Nights last month and could not get away from the swarms of horny NPC citizens trying to jump my noodle serving bones. Baldur's Gate 3 launched with a bug that made your companions fuckable in just a few nights, and people didn't even notice. They thought: that's normal and right, I should shag everyone, gender and orientation be damned. See that mountain? You can fuck it. And that's (at least partially) thanks to Bioware.

GTA is an unignorable thing. It is one of those breakout cultural objects that has its own gravity, drawing in attention and comment from politicians, mainstream press, parents, schools, comedians, columnists, footballers, taxi drivers, and hairdressers. In all the weight of it, I hadn't yet really seen it as a game. Simon Parkin's Edge cover feature may not reveal many new details about the game but it has made me appreciate it as a game (and maybe even get a little bit excited for its eventual PC release.

Nelson, grave-faced but friendly, wearing all black, with grey-flecked stubble, settles into a leather-and-chrome Eames chair while we perch on a burnt-orange sofa facing a pair of expansive wall-mounted TVs. In the past, Rockstar has carefully stage-managed encounters such as this. For previews of previous GTAs, one team member played the game while a publicist read from a pre-prepared script, further evidence of the paranoia that can take hold when an artist is working on something the entire world is desperate to see.

Today, however, Nelson has no script and, apparently, no plan. For the next 90 minutes he simply plays the current build, following his nose, confident that the game's systems will hold together wherever he pushes them, that this world's glories will glint and shimmer no matter which angle he approaches from. It is an extraordinary demonstration not of paranoia but of trust – in the game, in the team that built it, perhaps even in us.

Nelson picks up the controller and lets Grand Theft Auto VI speak for itself.

I am guilty of forgetting and looking away, but the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has not ended, it is deepening. Writing for the LRB, Selma Dabbagh bluntly captures the ugly events of the past two years :

In January 2025 Donald Trump described Gaza as a ‘demolition site’. ‘You’re talking about probably a million and a half people,’ he said, ‘and we just clean out that whole thing.’ The number is closer to two million people – not a ‘whole thing’ but two million individual human beings – who have been driven into an area that’s less than a third of the densely inhabited land they lived on. Their cities and arable lands – palms, olives, coriander, citrus and pomegranate trees – have been obliterated.

I'd like there to be a big reason for this week's music recommendation, but really it's just a little victory lap. I managed to nab some tickets to see This Is The Kit, so give Bashed Out a listen, yeah?

World of Warcraft: Forever's launch has been downright impressive—MMOs are notoriously difficult to run servers for, particularly when it comes to launch, where players will get bottlenecked into servers, throwing devs into a catch 22: Do they increase capacity and wind up wasting money in the long run while things die down, or do they ride out the wave? And yet, after the chaos of the beta, it's been buttery smooth.

Which is why I'm willing to forgive Blizzard for a weird quirk of its realmless layering technology—cities have been empty, empty as hell. Which is a shame, given I know that hundreds of thousands of players are technically on this thing—and yet, none of them are in my Stormwind.

Well, Forever's devs are working on a fix, per the official forums: "Just wanted to chime in," says Aggrend, "And say that we are aware of some issues with certain areas not feeling as populated as they should. We will be tweaking some numbers tomorrow to help things feel a bit more lively. Thanks for the feedback on this one!"

That's a relief to hear, especially given I'm on a roleplay server, and there have been problems with this sort of thing where phasing has interrupted the flow of narrative commerce in the past. Cities, especially, should feel lived-in, and it's hard to create a sense of community when people you could be writing with keep bamfing in and out of existence.

But even if you aren't a roleplayer like yours truly, I think you should be gladdened by this news—big cities are one of the places where crowding isn't a problem at all, but rather, the thing you want. They're social hubs, and rubbing shoulder to shoulder with the masses at the auction house is kind of the whole point.

At least anecdotally, my Stormwind's been looking a lot more populated, and I'm sure that as populations settle to sane levels and Blizzard keeps chipping away at this tech, the streets'll be bustling again.

#4002. Epic Games further doubles down on gen-AI tools for Fortnite, Unreal Engine 6 and more: "Our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code"

"We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism."

To no one's surprise, Epic Games has now confirmed that it's tripling down on its gen-AI push and will use the controversial tech on everything from Fortnite to the next iteration of its widely-used game development engine, Unreal Engine 6.

Speaking to This Week In Video Games, executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer confirmed that "we are definitely using AI to develop code and features for Unreal Engine," but that work will also be extended to the engine's next big numbered version. "Almost all development happening right now is being done in the dev streams attached to Fortnite, UEFN [Unreal Editor for Fortnite], and UE6."

When asked specifically if Epic is vibe-coding anything related to Unreal Engine, Wassmer put it plainly: "Yes, we are vibe-coding things. That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We're not 'one-shotting' the engine; we're iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes." Wassmer claimed the AI tools would help the company push out updates faster and with fewer bugs.

Epic seemingly isn't sweating over the divisive reaction to its gen-AI push, either - even as workers worry about job security, developers worry about plagiarism, and communities across the world worry about its environmental impact. Wassmer explained the company is "more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism."

"We don't think it's viable to take a halfway approach to AI in development," he added. "We think it's best to just be up front with what we're doing, share best practices with other developers, and make the best UE6 we can with the best tools available at any given time."

Earlier this month, Epic proudly admitted to vibe-coding the latest iteration of the Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to run slightly faster than Steam. "Prograaming is hard," the multi-billion dollar company explained at the time. "So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded the new Epic Games Launcher." Developers working on a troubled Disney and Marvel shooter were reportedly told to let gen-AI handle code and art production, too.

Epic CEO Tim Sweeney then started an online debate over Valve's AI policy that asks developers to disclose gen-AI use on their Steam pages. Sweeney argued that "forcing developers to write a political statement to be used against them by the hate mod they're helping organize is abhorrent." It's not surprising to see Epic dig its heels in further, then.

#4001. It looks like footage of a Persona 1 remake has leaked, and if it's legit I really hope you don't hate the colour purple

I'm sure the artist formerly known as Prince would have loved it, at least

In this genAI world, every single leak that makes its way out into the world should be seen as more of a "leak" until proven otherwise. With that said, it does kind of seem like a remake of the first Persona game is on the way, with some footage supposedly leaking and showing it in action.

The leaked footage was shared yesterday to the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, originally uploaded to the file-sharing site Gofile on Halloween, i.e. yesterday, i.e. October 31st. You will not at all be surprised to hear that, stylistically, it's incredibly in line with the vibe of contemporary Persona, a la the visual design established with Persona 5 that's been carried through to the Persona 3 and 4 remakes.

There's not a whole lot of footage to actually look at, just shy of two minutes all told. One bit shows the game's protagonist walking through a school at night before starting a battle. Again, the battle system looks like what you'd expect from Persona, being turn based and whatnot. The colour theme for this one is overwhelmingly purple, too, which at least lines up with the series' 25th anniversary artwork. What's perhaps slightly odd is that Persona 2's protagonist can be seen in battle; not sure if this is implying a combination of the two games, if two remakes are being made in tandem and it's a temporary use of assets, or if it's just an odd placeholder.

Persona 1 and 2 remakes wouldn't exactly be much of a surprise. Ashley interviewed series producer Kazuhisa Wada not too long ago, and he literally said "Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too." A knowing tease from Wada, perhaps? Who knows! Either way, the gameplay on display here looks believable, and Sega's leakier than a broken faucet (various Persona bits have leaked in the past too), so, something to keep an eye on at the very least, even if best taken with a pinch of salt.

#4000. More Chinese success as Phantom Blade Zero enjoys a big launch and becomes one of Steam's most played games

Phantom Blade Zero has been officially released, and just as everyone expected, it's popular. The wuxia action game from S-Game debuted to a massive 431,541 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB) at its peak just hours ago.

At the time of writing, Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's second most-played game, landing just below Counter-Strike 2, and it's currently leading Steam's global top sellers chart, having jumped 16 places this week. Players appear to be happy with the final game, too, judging by early user reviews on Steam, which currently have it sitting at a Mostly Positive average.

S-Game has yet to announce any sales figures, but the game was estimated to have sold more than 1m copies just before launch. According to Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott, Phantom Blade Zero sold 850,000 copies across PC and PlayStation 5. It is also available on Tencent WeGame in China, where Elliott estimates it sold enough to bring the total to well above 1m copies.

A few days earlier, Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold 500,000 on Steam. The analyst indicated that 80,000 copies were sold after reviews were published two days before the game's 28th October release. As impressive as all of that is, it pales in comparison to Black Myth: Wukong's sales performance - another Chinese-developed action title. When Wukong released in 2024, the game peaked at 2,415,714 concurrent players on Steam, and is estimated to have sold over 30m copies lifetime.

Elliott said on X he doesn't believe Phantom Blade Zero will be able to achieve that level of success, but he predicts strong sales this year regardless - which is already borne out by the available data.

Seeing as the game has benefited from the pre-launch hype, word of mouth may help boost these numbers further. By the weekend, we could be looking at well above 500,000 peak concurrents on Steam.

In Eurogamer's review of Phantom Blade Zero, Emma Kent lamented a general lack of polish and pace-breaking boss fights, which put a dampener on her enjoyment of the best parts of the game: swordplay and combat.

#3998. Dog poo, anti-social behaviour, and Jason: Our latest look at GTA 6 gameplay comes from an episode of South Park

So we know that GTA 6 has a marketing deal with Sony and the PlayStation 5, and that Rockstar has been engaging with real-world locations to get the word about its latest sandbox game out into the world ahead of its 19th November launch. But it seems the reach of Rockstar's marketing arm has no limit, as brand new gameplay footage cropped up in a quite unexpected place last night: the latest episode of South Park.

On Wednesday night (28th October), the latest episode of South Park (which is currently going by the name 'South America', as a jab at President Trump and his insistence on renaming landmarks and locations) aired on Comedy Central, and it included a quick snippet of new gameplay for GTA 6. Eurogamer has seen the episode, and can verify the authenticity of the footage. Rockstar Games is thanked in the credits, too.

#GTAVI Uncut version of the 🐶💩 (+cropped) pic.twitter.com/mxGB9z7fCn

As for context for the gameplay footage, it pops up when Cartman, Kyle, Stan, Randy Marsh (with a more youthful appearance, thanks to events earlier in the series), and Butters' father Steven Stoch are sitting around the table as a woman presents the footage to the assembled crew. The setup is that the woman has managed to obtain 'smuggled' footage of Grand Theft Auto 6, the release of which poses and existential threat to the USA as it launches around the Midterm elections. "November is coming," she says. "And everyone's freaking out because we have to choose who will be in charge when we're all dealing with something that we are not prepared for!"

We cut to the gameplay. "See the world-building?" asks the woman, as a German Shepherd poos on a crowded beach. "Look at that, the graphics are seriously next-level. It's a dog, taking a poop. And people can pick up the dog poop! You can throw things at the person with dog poop. And if they choose to fight back, you can pick up the dog poop, and actually attack them with the dog poop. That... is what's coming in November."

The boys, predictably, are impressed. We only really see Jason picking up some poo and then attacking a pedestrian with it, but hey - it's something right? GTA 6 has been a recurring part of South Park's most recent season, as the whole world holds its breath for November. "Don't worry," characters repeatedly say, "everything will be better in November... that's when GTA 6 comes out." Indeed.

There's been a lot of information about GTA 6 to take in lately: whether it's the whispers of a PC version arriving in Q1 2027, the massive PS5 file size, or the fact Rockstar workers are voting to unionise over the release window of the game, it's a busy time for the game. Don't expect that hype to die down as we edge closer to GTA 6's release: it's going to be a massive thing for games, and modern culture as a whole.

#3997. What remains of canned Portal prequel white whale F-Stop is now fully playable thanks to modders and some big leaks

If you're something of a Portal or Half-Life head, you'll probably already be familiar with F-Stop, an unreleased Portal prequel that remained quite mysterious for many years. Back in 2020, a much deeper look was revealed in a semi-official capacity, revealing a pretty neat concept (that isn't so dissimilar to that of Superliminal). Now, all these years later, assets and source code for the game has leaked, and what exists of F-Stop is fully playable.

As spotted by Kotaku, the Valve Cut Content team and a number of leakers have been able to put together a playable version of F-Stop so that you can try it out for yourself. Mechanically, it works like so: you take a picture of an object, and said object disappears, turning it into a photo. You can then use this photo to rematerialise the object, sometimes changing the scale of it to help you navigate particular puzzles. It's cool! Just not something Valve thought was worth going all in on, evidently.

So the story goes, Valve overlord Gabe Newell did actually quite like the early version of the game that never was, it's just it didn't test all that well. I do kind of think that this is a lesson in not always listening to test audiences; the aforementioned Superliminal really is quite similar in execution, even tonally it's on the same kind of wavelength, and it ended up being quite a tight little experience that ended up being received quite positively, generally. In the end, bits of F-Stop were Frankensteined into Portal 2, so, at least we got that out of it!

The reason for the delay in being able to play F-Stop in this unofficial capacity is because of the crucial source code and map data. Back in August about 12TB of Steam data leaked, but that only contained the assets for F-Stop. Mods in the Valve Cut Content Discord server said that the person who leaked the F-Stop mapsrc asked for $1000 before just handing over the data in any case. Glad they did, $1000 bucks is a lot, I wouldn't pay it myself. Cool little bit of history to be found here, shame it never materialised in the way it was meant to.

Sony has indefinitely delayed the PS5’s official Pulse Elevate desktop speakers, which were originally due to deploy days from now, on 12th November.

This delay feels eerily similar to the one that affected its FlexStrike arcade stick earlier in the year, which was originally due out on 6th August but ultimately indefinitely postponed.

At the time, the manufacturer said it had encountered “unexpected production delays”, but that was several months ago now and it hasn’t provided an update since.

Sony’s Edwin Foo said of the Pulse Elevate delay:

Remember when Grand Theft Auto 6 was delayed, not once but twice? It's hard to forget: its first release date was treated as a day of mourning by some particularly upset fans. Despite all the outcries from fans, Take-Two Interactive chief Strauss Zelnick has repeatedly explained that he doesn't regret the decision.

Talking to WSJ the interviewer asks Zelnick what his immediate emotion was after hearing from the team that GTA 6 needed to be delayed: "I don't always feel calm but I tend to come across as calm … The timing of the call was not great for an array of reasons. We had just had a board retreat 10 days earlier so I wasn't thrilled about the timing. That said, this is a balancing act with all creative executives and it's not just time, it could be resources."

"These are very difficult decisions to make," Zelnick continues. "If, on the other hand, if as a refresher course, your mission is to make the best entertainment on earth and part of your three part strategy is to be the most creative, sometimes you have to make these expensive and inconvenient decisions in service of that mission goal.

The delay was essential, Zelnick says, to stay true to Take-Two's mission "to make the best entertainment on earth."

"What happens when people take the other approach," Zelnick asks. "The other approach being we're slavishly devoted to a schedule and we're just going to ship despite what is going on. I'm not going to throw any competitors under the bus, but if you know anything about the videogame business in the past few years there was a very high profile release that fell into this category. They shipped and they had to pull the title after shipping because it didn't work."

I don't think there's much doubt about what game Zelnick is referencing here, but just in case anyone is wondering, my bet would be on Concord—yeah, it's probably Concord. And for good reason: it didn't have a shred of the anticipation that GTA 6 has but was still bankrolled by a major studio and essentially burnt hundreds of millions of dollars—a cautionary tale if ever I heard one.

#3994. Modern Warfare 4 faces backlash after real footage of South Korean crowd crush tragedy was discovered in game's opening moments

Bereaved families demand the removal of these clips.

Activision has come under fire due to the inclusion of real-world footage of the tragic Itaewon Disaster in Modern Warfare 4. The bereaved families association and the Citizens Countermeasure Meeting are asking for the footage to be removed.

In its opening moments, short clips are used to represent a news report of fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. These include archived news clips of a person being carried away on a stretcher, someone performing CPR on a victim, and multiple bodies laying on a road.

"Using such an incident as material for a game intended for entertainment purposes is itself highly inappropriate and a senseless act," the groups said in a joint statement (thanks SBS news).

"The Itaewon tragedy was a tragic disaster that produced hundreds of casualties, and citizens who participated in the rescue efforts or witnessed the event at the time continue to suffer from trauma. If the game developer has even a minimum level of courtesy and empathy toward the victims, they should promptly take corrective measures."

This statement was joined by another by The Korean Game Consumers Association, who wrote: "There must be a clear explanation of the circumstances and an apology regarding the fact that footage of a tragic disaster unrelated to the context of gameplay was utilized, causing harm to the bereaved families and others." It called for the footage to be replaced in an update, while also emphasising the controversy should not grow into a demand for censorship of the game.

Eurogamer contacted Activision for comment, and was provided the following statement: "In developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect. The game’s opening cinematic utilizes some real world news coverage to establish the game’s fictional narrative. It is not intended to reference or trivialize the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form."

Today is the four year anniversary of the Itaewon crowd crush tragedy, in which 160 people died and a further 196 were injured. It is South Korea's most severe mass casualty event since the Sampoong Department Store collapse in 1995.

#3993. Dune: Awakening's seasonally appropriate Blood and Ice expansion gets a December release date, and in a plus for preservation, an offline mode this month

December is certainly going to be the month of Dune. The biggest Dune of Dunecember will obviously go to Dune: Part 3, which is Duen out December 18th. A little bit before that, however, is a well-timed free expansion coming to Dune: Awakening. It's called Blood and Ice, which sounds gross, but hey, I guess free blood and ice isn't entirely a bad thing?

"The expansion introduces the Polar Sink, an entirely new survival map where everything you've learned about surviving in the desert will be put to the test," explains a Steam blog post. "Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm. The technology you've developed to survive the desert won't be enough here, and you'll need to upgrade your equipment, gather new resources, and adapt your strategies to survive the cold."

You'll find two biomes in the Polar Sink, the tundra and the ice cap, the former being where you'll kick off your time in this expansion. "While conditions here are more manageable than on the ice cap itself, these families won't welcome anyone interfering with their operations," the blog notes. Your main goal is to get the ice cap and gather up all of its valuable resources, namely, ice! Said ice can then be used to "cool your base equipment and speed up production."

Apparently you'll get about 35 more hours of "new progression, along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialization traits," out of the expansion, and there are plans for future updates that'll give you reason to come back to the Polar Sink in Duen time. Beyond that, there is also a new cosmetic store, which lets you purchase "optional cosmetic items, including outfits, vehicle variants, and additional ways to customize your bases." I'm sure this will go down well.

Perhaps most importantly, this November will see the arrival of offline mode, meaning you don't need an internet connection to play it. Hopefully if (probably when (sorry to be a pessimist (realist))) the servers go down, this means it'll still be playable. Character copying so that you can copy your character from multiplayer servers to single-player will be coming in January, alongside full cross-play. Lots coming essentially!

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is finally out in the wild a good 28 years after Nintendo's original gem dropped back in 1998, and is already proving to be the highest-rated game of 2026 thus far.

Sure, it's a remake, but it slots in nicely between all the other new games – and it's still just as valuable, too, as Nintendo senior vice president of product development and publishing Nate Bihldorff explains to Polygon. "I do think that new games and remakes both have a place in the Nintendo stable, of equal importance to be honest. There are fans of every single IP that we have out there," as he says. Remakes are very welcome to those fans, to say the least.

"Of course, having new games in those series is wonderful, and I look forward to them as much as anyone else does, but there's also a deep satisfaction in revisiting games that were very, very special, like Ocarina of Time" – and that's evident in how well the remake is doing already, if you ask me. It made Metacritic's top 30 games of all time within a day, proving that the community is very much happy to enjoy remakes as it is entirely fresh titles.

Longtime Legend of Zelda fans aren't the only people immersing themselves in Nintendo's revamped spin on Hyrule, either. As Bihldorff states, "It's also important to think about how many people had never played the original, and for them, the remake of Ocarina of Time is going to be an absolutely brand-new, 2026 experience, and one that I just cannot wait for them to get their hands on." A quick look at social media proves his assertion here right.

Remakes don't just cater to old fans, but they help introduce countless more to long-standing franchises and series like The Legend of Zelda. They certainly don't take away from new releases, either – every fellow Zelda stan I know is on the edge of their seat waiting for more announcements from Nintendo, especially after the likes of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. I don't see that changing, ever.

#3991. Xbox leader Asha Sharma says there's "more demand than consoles available" as Xbox hardware sales dip by 14%

"We're making progress, with a lot more work ahead."

Xbox leader Asha Sharma has claimed there's "more demand than consoles available" when it comes to Xbox, and that console sales "remain constrained by supply".

She was speaking after Microsoft announced its quarterly financial results yesterday, in which Xbox revenue declined two percent year on year. The financials also revealed a drop in Xbox hardware sales, which are down 14 percent year-on-year, driven by a "lower volume of consoles sold".

Sharma's positive spin, which she posted on X, highlighted record-breaking performances of Minecraft and World of Warcraft: Forever, and applauded Call of Duty's "most acclaimed release in more than a decade". She also trumpeted double-digit revenue growth on PC.

"Console sales remain constrained by supply," Sharma added, "with more demand than consoles available. We're working to get more consoles into players' hands, including through our expanded refurbishment program. We're making progress, with a lot more work ahead."

In Microsoft's earnings call, transcribed by Seeking Alpha, company boss Satya Nadella also celebrated Minecraft's "record quarter" and World of Warcraft having "its largest beta in franchise history". In addition, Nadella pointed to "one of our strongest first- and third-party [holiday] lineups in years", name-dropping COD Modern Warfare 4 and GTA 6 as two of the reasons why. But there was no mention of Gears of War: E-Day, which, with a 6th October release date, does fall within that holiday period.

Microsoft chief financial officer Amy Hood added a bit more detail, noting that the dip in Xbox revenue was "driven by declines in third-party content and Xbox Game Pass, partially offset by growth in first-party content".

These Xbox results come not long after Asha Sharma said the Xbox division had "started to return to growth" following the drastic restructuring she has spearheaded, and that has resulted in more than 1800 job losses so far. That restructuring work is ongoing, by the way, with more waves of lay-offs expected soon, and as Microsoft more widely offers voluntary redundancy to many thousands of staff.

Overall, though, Microsoft appears to be prospering as a business, with its cloud services in particular driving notable gains in revenue and profit. But it's those cloud services that are also the cause of calls to boycott the company's products, because of their use by the Israeli military in the subjugation and ongoing genocide of Palestinians. It's a connection that recently resulted in Big Walk developer House House refusing to sell its game on Xbox.

#3990. Gag Order is a co-op, SCP-ish horror shooter about surviving as best you can against some nasty, tentacle covered cephalopod creatures

Don't let it touch me, please and thank you

What makes Carrion interesting obviously lies in playing as the monster in a horror game rather than being the one chased down by it. The game's nasty tentacle monster still gives me the heebie jeebies, so I really would hate to be hunted by one. This is where I point you towards Gag Order, a shooter where you are in fact hunted by a disgusting cephalopod creature all while tracking down a distress signal.

Gag Order is not designed to be played solo, it feels wrong to call it friendslop given how unfriendly it is in vibes, but it does feel like it fits into a similar lineage as Lethal Company at the very least. In it, you are a research lab's Guardian Unit member, and you get a distress call "from one of the core parts of the complex." Upon arrival, the atmosphere is rotten, and you quickly come to understand that you are not equipped for what you have to deal with.

The solution, then, is to take care of those nightmare-inducing cephalopod creatures. Except during the first phase of a run, it sounds like they're invincible. Your guns do seem to be able to fend them off at the very least, but it's the second phase, which is geared around a "fast paced team-bossight" where it sounds like you'll be trying to take these things down. I'm not quite sure what the process is to get between those two phases, but I'm quite fond of the vibes on display.

It feels a touch reminiscent of 2000s shooters with some slightly contemporary mechanical sensibilities. I'm fond of the light SCP vibes it has going on, alongside the faint surrealness of certain elements like a bunch of crows hanging out in an abandoned office building. Creepy! Good looking stuff. Gag Order is apparently due out by the end of 2026, though we're obviously getting close there, so it's worth keeping an eye on it by throwing it a wishlist on Steam, if it takes your fancy.

#3989. COD Modern Warfare 4's controversial Possum ability nerfed to stop it being used "as a combat mechanic instead of a survival mechanic"

Since the launch of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ mode, players have been mainly arguing about two topics: whether there's a need for a PvE-only mode, and whether Possum - an in-game trait - has a place in an extraction experience.

And developer Infinity Ward has clearly taken a side in the Possum argument by implementing a key change to how it works. In Modern Warfare 4's latest patch, released overnight, the developer made it so that Possum - an ability that can revive a player - cannot be activated while the team that killed you is nearby. Possum also can't be activated if it's been less than four minutes since you were killed.

These two should address the most common complaints, but Infinity Ward left space for further tweaks in the future, such as by adjusting its range and duration.

If you're unfamiliar, Possum allows a player to revive themselves from a completely dead state once per match. To other players around, you appear to be dead and your body can be looted. But by using Possum, clever players were able to exact immediate revenge on their killers - or anyone else standing around near their apparent corpse - by springing back to life and shooting them in the back.

Possum's intended use was for dead players to have another shot at extracting from the match, rather than forfeiting the run entirely. Though their loot may be lost, Possum allowed players to save their operator.

Infinity Ward underlined this intention in a note accompanying the change. "The intention for Possum is to give a high level operator a second chance," the developer said in a blog post. "With the current iteration, Possum was being used as a combat mechanic instead of a survival mechanic.

"These tweaks are meant to prevent players from getting right back into the fight which they had just lost. We will be watching the use of Possum with this change to see if it has the desired effect."

Outside of that DMZ change, the 28th October patch includes a round of weapon balance changes. There are several buffs to assault rifles and SMGs, and some nerfs to the APOC-338 and FiNN LMGs. The buffs are notable given the across-the-board nerf Infinity Ward experimented with during the second beta weekend for Modern Warfare 4, which sought to increase the time-to-kill (TTK) impact of weapons, making them feel weaker as a result.

The patch also fixes several bugs players have been able to exploit in multiplayer and DMZ. And, in case you missed it, this is the patch that adds the Shipment map to the game - and yes, there's a 24/7 playlist.

Eurogamer's full review of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is due later today.
